content: When the population of children under 10 years of age in a specific area is less than 1,100, all children in that area should be tested using appropriate statistical methods for finite populations. Parasitological evaluations, such as skin snip microscopy and DEC patch tests, can be utilized to monitor progress during the initial treatment phase of onchocerciasis elimination programs. However, these methods are not suitable for verifying the elimination of the disease. The guidelines for certifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis, published by the WHO in 2001, were used to confirm the interruption of transmission in Colombia (2013), Ecuador (2014), and Mexico (2015). In Africa, transmission has been interrupted in certain areas (e.g., Mali, Senegal, Sudan, and Uganda), leading to the discontinuation of mass drug administration (MDA). Many countries are now planning to determine whether they have successfully eliminated the transmission of Onchocerca volvulus. Additionally, the guidelines were updated to align with international standards as outlined in the second edition of the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2014). The criteria in these guidelines are intended for use at the end of the elimination process, when programs decide whether to stop MDA and transition to post-treatment surveillance and monitoring for potential disease recrudescence. Transmission interruption following MDA should only be considered achieved after adequate post-treatment surveillance has been completed in all endemic areas. Verification of parasite transmission elimination occurs at the end of a 3–5-year surveillance period. The guidelines aim to prepare endemic countries for stopping MDA at the end of the treatment phase (Phase 1), transitioning to post-treatment surveillance (Phase 2), and confirming the interruption of transmission at the end of Phase 2 and the beginning of post-elimination surveillance (Phase 3). The purpose of these guidelines is to provide an updated tool for achieving and verifying the elimination of O. volvulus transmission at the end of onchocerciasis elimination programs, primarily using MDA. The objectives of the guidelines are: 1. To provide evidence-based recommendations to health providers and policymakers for demonstrating and confirming the interruption of O. volvulus transmission before, during, and after post-treatment surveillance. 2. To inform end-users of the procedures required for verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis. The target audience includes policymakers in endemic countries, national neglected tropical disease or onchocerciasis elimination programs, and those involved in verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis. The guidelines were developed in accordance with the 2014 WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. Two key questions were formulated: 1. Which diagnostic tests or combinations of tests can validly and reliably demonstrate the interruption of O. volvulus transmission for the purpose of stopping MDA? 2. Which diagnostic tests or combinations of tests can validly and reliably confirm the interruption of O. volvulus transmission at the end of post-treatment surveillance? Experts conducted a systematic review of the literature, and the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach was used to assess the evidence and formulate recommendations. The GRADE approach assigns a level of confidence (high, moderate, low, or very low) to the evidence supporting each outcome. Recommendations were formulated based on the balance of benefits and harms, resource requirements, cost, equity, feasibility, and acceptability. The recommendations include: 1. The O-150 PCR (Poolscreen) test in black flies should be used to demonstrate the interruption of O. volvulus transmission in human populations receiving MDA. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty of evidence. 2. The Ov-16 serology test should be used in children under 10 years of age to demonstrate the interruption of O. volvulus transmission in human populations receiving MDA. This is a strong recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 3. Skin snip microscopy should not be used to demonstrate the interruption of O. volvulus transmission in human populations receiving MDA. However, it may be used during a transition to Ov-16 serology, with both methods applied in parallel. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 4. Assessment of ocular infection should not be used to demonstrate the interruption of O. volvulus transmission in human populations receiving MDA. This is a strong recommendation with low certainty of evidence. To confirm the interruption of O. volvulus transmission at the end of post-treatment surveillance: 1. O-150 PCR (Poolscreen) testing in black flies should be used. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty of evidence. 2. The Ov-16 serology test should be used in children when the O-150 PCR results are at or near the threshold (e.g., less than 1 L3 infectious larva per 2,000 flies). This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 3. Assessment of ocular infection should not be used to confirm the interruption of O. volvulus transmission. This is a strong recommendation with low certainty of evidence. Stopping MDA requires four steps: 1. The health ministry establishes an independent oversight committee to address matters related to onchocerciasis elimination. 2. The committee advises the country to stop MDA based on the guidelines, considering factors such as lymphatic filariasis treatment status, cross-border risks, and the length of post-treatment surveillance. 3. The committee advises the national program to prepare a country report once all foci have completed the post-treatment surveillance period. 4. The country submits its report to WHO through the appropriate regional office. Post-elimination surveillance involves regular O-150 PCR assessments of black flies in countries where WHO has verified elimination, continuing until the risk of disease recrudescence is eliminated in the entire region. Future considerations include the potential revision of these guidelines by 2020, based on new diagnostic tools, interventions, or improved metrics generated by modeling-based research on onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis. Human onchocerciasis, caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus, is a vector-borne disease endemic in 31 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, three countries in Latin America, and Yemen. Chronic infection leads to severe itching, disfiguring skin lesions, and irreversible blindness. The disease is transmitted by black flies of the genus Simulium, which breed in fast-flowing rivers and streams, earning the disease the name river blindness. In the Americas, it is also known as Robles’ disease, named after Dr. Rodolfo Robles, who first documented the causal relationship between O. volvulus and vision loss. In Africa, the disease has significant socioeconomic consequences, including the abandonment of fertile land near vector breeding sites. Control strategies have included nodule removal, vector control, and mass drug administration (MDA) with ivermectin. MDA with ivermectin, administered annually or semi-annually, is the primary intervention in most programs. Community-directed treatment with ivermectin is the main strategy of the African Programme for Onchocerciasis Control (APOC), established in 1995. In the Americas, semi-annual MDA with ivermectin, with a minimum coverage of 85% of the eligible population, is the adopted strategy.
